about.title: Delano Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Delano's economy runs on agriculture, packing, transport, and the local businesses that support them, and workers in these fields face real physical risks every shift. When an injury happens, California law generally routes claims through workers' compensation regardless of fault, which can leave workers wondering why their employer isn't directly liable. But that's not always the end of the story. If a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver contributed to the injury, a separate third-party claim may be possible alongside workers' comp benefits. This matters in Kern County's mixed industrial and agricultural work sites, where multiple companies and contractors often share the same jobsite. LawProactive doesn't file claims or offer legal advice ourselves; we connect injured workers with an independent attorney who can look at the details of what happened, explain how workers' comp and third-party claims interact, and help figure out what applies to your situation.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About a Workplace Injury

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Picture
items.desc: California generally treats workers' comp as the exclusive remedy against an employer, but a negligent third party like a subcontractor or equipment maker can still be pursued separately.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Matter
items.desc: Workplace injuries generally need to be reported to your employer within 30 days, and missing that window can complicate your benefits.

items.title: Retaliation Protections Exist
items.desc: California law prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who report injuries or file claims, which can matter if you're worried about your job.

items.question: Can I file a claim if I was injured on a Delano job site involving multiple contractors?
items.answer: Possibly. When several companies operate on the same site, a third party separate from your direct employer may share responsibility for unsafe conditions. An independent attorney can review the details to see whether a claim beyond workers' comp applies.

items.question: What if my employer says I waited too long to report my injury?
items.answer: California generally requires injuries to be reported within 30 days, so timing matters. An attorney can review your specific circumstances and explain your options even if there was a delay.

items.question: Does workers' comp cover everything, or should I also consider a separate claim?
items.answer: Workers' comp typically covers medical costs and partial wage replacement, but it doesn't account for full damages a third party might owe. If equipment, another driver, or a property owner contributed to your injury, a separate claim could be worth exploring alongside your workers' comp benefits.
